The Data-Type Ontology

Source: vignettes/data-type-ontology.Rmd
data-type-ontology.Rmd

Why “it’s a number” is not enough

Suppose you load a survey file into R and one column looks like this:

47401
06037
90210

R will probably call this column numeric. But that label is not just unhelpful, it is dangerous:

  • 06037 is a county code (Los Angeles County). Treated as a number, its leading zero disappears and it becomes 6037 — a different, wrong code.
  • 47401 is a ZIP code. You would never want its average.
  • If you save the column and a colleague reopens it in Excel, the zeros vanish again and the codes are quietly corrupted.

So “what type is this?” is really three questions at once: how should the value be treated (is it a quantity you can add up, or a label you must leave alone?), what does it mean (a ZIP? a county?), and how is it written (five digits with a leading zero that must survive)? A single type word cannot answer all three.

formex answers them by placing each column in a small, shared catalog of data types — the ontology. Think of “ontology” as nothing fancier than a labeled map of every kind of column research data contains, together with the instructions for handling each one. Two functions read this same map: guess_data_type() (which figures out where a column belongs) and fx_stabilize() (which cleans the column up using the instructions stored there).

o <- fx_ontology()
dim(o)   # one row per written form of a type; columns described below
#> [1] 97 29

Typing is walking down a decision tree

The map is organized as a decision tree. Typing a column means starting at the top and walking down, answering one narrowing question at a time. Each step down is more specific than the last:

LEVEL 1  data_type         how should it be treated?     number · text · temporal · ...
LEVEL 2  semantic_family   what broad kind within that?  date · currency · geographic · ...
LEVEL 3  semantic_type     what exactly does it mean?    calendar date · US dollars · ...
LEVEL 4  format_style      how is it written? / + unit_type: what unit is it in?

Here is the walk for a column of dates like 03/15/2019:

  1. Level 1 — data_type. These are not words, counts, or categories; they are points in time. → temporal.
  2. Level 2 — semantic_family. Within time, is it a clock time, a span, a calendar date? → date.
  3. Level 3 — semantic_type. A plain calendar date (not a fiscal quarter, not a timestamp with a clock). → calendar.
  4. Level 4 — format_style. How is the date written? Month first, with slashes. → mdy_slash.

Getting to level 4 is the goal, and it is worth saying why.

Why the bottom of the tree matters

Only at level 4 does formex know enough to handle the column safely. “Safely” means three specific things, and all three need the exact written form:

  • Read it in correctly. 03/15/2019 has to be parsed as March 15, not as some other order. You cannot know the order until you are at the leaf.
  • Clean it up (stabilize it). Rewrite every value into one standard form — here, the unambiguous 2019-03-15 — so the column is consistent.
  • Write it back without future corruption. Store it so that when anyone reopens the file — in R, in Excel, years later — it loads back as the right thing, with no lost leading zeros, no numbers silently turned into dates, no dates silently turned into numbers.

That last point is the whole payoff. A column that has reached level 4 can be put into a protected form: a value plus a stored rule for re-reading it, so the file is self-describing and cannot be corrupted by a careless reopen. (The Guessing a Column’s Type vignette walks through this “stabilizing” step in detail.) A column stuck higher up the tree can still be stored, but only under a more cautious, general rule.

Level 4 is really two questions: how it’s written, and what unit it’s in

Older versions of formex had a single label at the bottom of the tree. Version 7 splits it into two, because they are genuinely different questions:

  • format_style — how the value is written. The same date can appear as 03/15/2019, 2019-03-15, or 15 Mar 2019. Same date, three writing styles. Style controls how you read the value in and how you write it back out.
  • unit_type — what the value is measured in. 2300 could be dollars or euros; 20 could be Celsius or Fahrenheit; 2019 could be a calendar year or a fiscal year. The unit does not change how the value is written, but it changes what it means — and whether converting it (say, Celsius to Fahrenheit) is even possible.

Sometimes you only need one. A plain calendar date has a writing style but no meaningful unit. A temperature reading has a unit (°C) that matters more than its writing. Reaching either one counts as getting to level 4, because either is enough to handle the column.

Failure is meant to be graceful

Real data is messy, and often the values simply do not say enough to reach the bottom. A column of bare five-digit numbers could be ZIPs, counties, or counts — nothing in the values themselves decides. formex is designed to stop at the lowest level it can actually defend, rather than guess and risk corrupting the column.

This is the key design principle: each level has a fallback. If formex cannot name the exact writing style, it still knows the family or the broad type, and can fall back to the safe, general rule for that level:

  • Reached level 4? Use the exact recipe — the best, lossless handling.
  • Only level 3 or 2? Apply the family’s general rule (e.g. “it’s a date of some kind — keep it as text but flag it for a human to confirm the format”).
  • Reached only level 1, or nothing at all? Fall all the way back to the safest possible rule: treat the value as plain text and change nothing. The original value is preserved exactly.

So the worst case is never corruption — it is simply a column left untouched, marked “I’m not sure,” waiting for a person or a data dictionary to settle it. A confident wrong guess would be far more damaging than an honest “this far and no further,” so the tree always prefers to stop early.

# a clean date column reaches the leaf (depth 4)
guess_data_type(c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020"))$route$depth
#> [1] 4
# a column of bare numbers cannot be pinned down -> it stops short
guess_data_type(c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5"))$route$depth
#> [1] 3

The depth number above is exactly how far down the tree the column got: 4 = all the way to the writing style, 3 = the specific meaning, 2 = the family, 1 = the broad type, 0 = unknown.

The whole tree

Here is the actual map, built live from the installed ontology, read as data_type → family : the specific types inside it:

boolean

  • binary — indicator, mixed, presence, response, status

categorical

  • multiselect — tags
  • mutually_exclusive — classification_code, geographic, missingness_reason, ordered, unordered
  • scale — grade_level, likert, ranking, rating

identifier

  • id — administrative, entity, geographic, hash, record, version

number

  • coordinate — lat, lat_lon, lon, lon_lat
  • currency — balance, euro, usd
  • portion — odds, percent, percentile, probability
  • quantity — count, duration, index, measurement, rank, rate, ratio, score
  • range — confidence_interval, min_max

structured

  • collection — array, list
  • geometry — point, polygon
  • record — key_value, object

temporal

  • date — calendar, timestamp
  • interval — date_range
  • period — month, quarter, reporting_period, year
  • phase — day_of_week, hour_of_day, month_of_year, week_of_year
  • time — clock

text

  • color — cmyk, color_name, hex, hsl, rgb
  • contact — email, phone
  • name — handle, organization, person, place
  • postal — full, po_box, street
  • text — label, literal, long, serialized, title
  • web — domain, ip, mac, url

unknown

  • unknown — heterogeneous, malformed, unclassified

How a type is spotted from the values

Not every type can be recognized just by looking at the values, and the ontology is honest about which can. Each type records how it is detected, in a column called match_kind:

match_kind rows
genome 3
lexicon 11
mask 49
mask+lexicon 7
none 15
shape 12
match_kind spotted by examples
genome a flexible date/time reader that tries many formats calendar, timestamp, clock
mask a fixed written shape, sometimes with a self-checking digit ein, isbn, phone, usd
lexicon membership in a known list of allowed values us_state, iso_country, first_name
mask+lexicon the right shape and a match in a known list person (looks like a name and is a known name)
shape the overall look of the numbers count, ratio, probability
none cannot be told from the values alone — only context can record keys, free text, unknown

The last row is important for honesty. A membership-number column is just integers; a notes column is just text. No amount of looking at the values will reveal what they are — that only comes from the column’s name or a data dictionary. The ontology marks these none so the engine knows not to pretend.

The handling instructions stored at each leaf

Once a column reaches a leaf, the ontology hands back the recipe for handling it safely — four short instructions written in formex’s little expression language (the {{ ... }} notation; the Formex vignette is the full guide):

column what it tells you example
data_format the pattern the raw file uses {{ mmddyyyy }}
raw_to_stable_transform how to rewrite it into the clean standard form {{ as_mmddyyyy }}
stable_format what that clean form looks like 2019-03-15
stable_import_rule how to re-read the clean value as the right type {{ as_yyyymmdd }}

A few real leaves, straight from the ontology:

semantic_type format_style match_kind data_format raw_to_stable_transform stable_format
calendar calendar genome {{ mmddyyyy }} {{ as_mmddyyyy }} 2019-03-15 ;; 2019-03-15
administrative ein mask {{ gov:ein }} {{ as_ein }} 12-3456789
usd usd mask {{ [strip:$,][range:-Inf,Inf][dec:.2] }} {{ as_usd }} {{ as_usd }} -45.00 ;; 2300.00 ;; 17298.00
person first_name lexicon {{ lexicon:given_name }} lookup:given given_name
count count shape {{ [range:0,Inf][dec:.0] }} {{ as_integer }} {{ as_integer }} 0 ;; 1 ;; 42

The split between the last two instructions has a purpose. The rewrite step (raw_to_stable_transform) is lossless and helps everyone downstream, so formex pushes as much work there as it can. The re-reading step (stable_import_rule) is held back for the one thing a plain CSV reader gets wrong on its own: forcing a value to stay the right type — a ZIP that must stay a label, a county code that must keep its leading zero — so the file survives the next reopen.

A couple of extra fields round out a leaf:

  • desired_default_format — the writing style to use when nobody states a preference (for a calendar date, ISO yyyymmdd).
  • validation, default_storage, short_desc — a plain-English description, the R storage class the cleaned value lands in, and the checks a value should pass.

When two branches both fit: the tie-breaker

Occasionally a column fits two leaves equally well. A column of city names could reasonably be a place name (free text) or a geographic grouping (a category you’d analyze by). The values alone cannot decide. For these known overlaps the ontology stores a tie-breaker rule in a disambiguator column, and the engine applies it. The current rule is cardinality — whether the values repeat or are unique:

# repeating city values read as a grouping; mostly-unique values read as names
guess_data_type(c("Chicago","Boston","Chicago","Austin","Boston","Chicago","Austin","Boston"))$route$data_type
#> [1] "categorical"
guess_data_type(c("Chicago","Boston","Austin","Denver","Miami","Seattle","Portland","Atlanta"))$route$data_type
#> [1] "text"

Putting it together in R

guess_data_type() walks a column down the tree and reports where it landed, as a $route — only as far down as it is sure:

r <- guess_data_type(c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020", "01/01/2021"))$route
r[c("data_type", "semantic_family", "semantic_type", "format_style", "depth")]
#> $data_type
#> [1] "temporal"
#> 
#> $semantic_family
#> [1] "date"
#> 
#> $semantic_type
#> [1] "calendar"
#> 
#> $format_style
#> [1] "mdy_slash"
#> 
#> $depth
#> [1] 4

fx_stabilize() then takes that landing spot and runs the stored recipe, returning the cleaned values and the rule for reloading them safely:

fx_stabilize(c("California", "TX", "Ohio"), "geographic", "us_state")[
  c("stable", "stable_format", "import_rule")]
#> $stable
#> [1] "CA" "TX" "OH"
#> 
#> $stable_format
#> [1] "usps_state"
#> 
#> $import_rule
#> [1] "{{ as_factor }}"

Because both functions read the same ontology, whatever guess_data_type() decides can be handed straight to fx_stabilize(). Every type also keeps a stable id (semantic_type_id like n0059, and variant_id like n0059-f01) that is assigned once and never reused, and old types are retired rather than deleted — so a label you recorded today still means the same thing years from now.
